title: How federal agencies can control costs and deliver mission value
summary: Agencies can bring some predictability to AI spending by governing consumption from design through day-to-day operations.
body_markdown:
By Richard Ross


Richard Ross


Director, Strategic Alliances


Richard Ross's Recent Articles


[Federal AI’s next test: Governing mission action, not just data](https://www.icf.com/insights/technology/governed-mission-action-ai)


Nov 17, 2026


6 MIN. READ


As AI becomes embedded in enterprise platforms, agencies must manage not only who has access, but the resources and costs of automated work. This makes solution design a budget decision, requiring mission, technology, acquisition, and financial leaders to govern AI consumption together.


For government technology executives, the challenge is no longer simply deploying AI, but demonstrating measurable mission value. As vendors build more generative and agentic AI capabilities into mission-critical platforms, leaders must contend with variable consumption costs alongside traditional seat-based licensing. What an AI agent does, how often it runs, and the resources it consumes all influence the cost of delivering mission outcomes. Realizing that value requires more disciplined consumption governance: forecasting demand, monitoring spend, and measuring results as AI scales.


## How to scale AI without losing fiscal control or mission value


Under seat-based licensing, cost follows headcount. An agency with 50 employees on a platform buys 50 licenses, and the annual bill is known in advance for the contracted seats and included capabilities. New capabilities arrive as new product SKUs, also priced in advance.


Under usage-based pricing, charges are based on what the workforce actually uses. They may align more closely with actual activity, although minimum commitments and expiring credits can still create unused spend. Agencies pay through consumption SKUs attached to a unit of activity, such as a token, a query, or an API call. Buying models also vary, including pay-as-you-go, committed spend, and prepaid credit pools drawn down as they are used.


Usage-based pricing can offer advantages. Under a per-seat model, an agency pays for 50 users, whether each one logs in daily or half never does.


The drawback is that the meter is tied to solution design. Depending on the platform and agreement, agent actions may trigger one or more consumption charges. A single workflow may draw on many meters at once. Document complexity, context size, retrieval volume, and the number of steps in an agent’s execution can all increase the burn rate. Because of this, cost architecture and solution architecture must be designed together.


Agencies can put controls in place, such as usage thresholds, monitoring, and human review points. Those controls, however, are not always built into the platform. An agency that deploys autonomous agents can easily incur unplanned costs under a pay-as-you-go contract or exhaust a prepaid credit pool before the solution delivers value.


## Why usage-based pricing presents challenges for agencies


Private companies face the same volatility, but for agencies, usage-based pricing creates three distinct risks:


**1. Budget execution risk:** Consumption can change faster than funding can be adjusted. An unexpectedly large bill may be an unwelcome surprise for a private company; for an agency, uncontrolled consumption can create funding control risks, including potential Antideficiency Act implications if obligations or expenditures exceed legally available funding.


**2. Timing and utilization risk:** Prepaid credits may expire before they are used, and their terms may not align with an agency’s funding calendar or contract period. Some allocations expire monthly instead of rolling over across the contract year. In that case, an agency can strand unused capacity in low-volume months while paying overages during seasonal peaks. Credits that expire may represent lost purchasing value, depending on the agreement’s expiration, rollover, refund, and reallocation terms.


**3. Acquisition and price analysis risk:** Agencies often estimate and structure technology costs around predictable quantities such as seat counts. Variable consumption introduces new complexity for independent government cost estimates (IGCEs), contract line-item numbers (CLINs), and firm-fixed-price (FFP) arrangements because it complicates workload assumptions, quantity estimates, price comparisons, and risk allocation.


## 4 ways agencies can manage costs while capturing AI value


Agencies can bring some predictability to AI spending by governing consumption from design through day-to-day operations. This helps leaders control costs while maintaining mission value. Four practices can help.


### Select and design for mission value


Use AI where it offers a measurable advantage over conventional automation, and choose the least costly model capable of meeting the mission requirement. Within a workflow, reserve metered AI for tasks that require interpretation or reasoning. Handle predictable, rule-based steps, such as routine record updates, with standard automation when it can meet the need.


Design choices also determine an agency’s level of dependence on a single vendor. Keeping agent logic portable preserves future options. Agencies can store prompts and business rules outside any single platform; connect systems through open, standard interfaces rather than platform-specific tools; and draw on their own data sources wherever possible. They can also build on infrastructure they’ve already paid for rather than automatically defaulting to bundled platform services.


Bring-your-own model options can add flexibility, but they don’t always remove the platform’s AI consumption charge. Agencies should track the costs of the underlying model, the platform’s AI meter, and any data or infrastructure use separately.


### Forecast demand


Estimate consumption before a price is finalized. Count how many AI actions each workflow takes to produce one result, such as resolving a case or processing an application, then multiply it by the expected volume. Plan for peak months, not just annual averages.


Pilots can replace planning assumptions with real data on burn rates and how often AI can complete a task without human handoff. Where trial credits are available, agencies can use proofs of concept to test consumption before making a larger commitment.


The agency’s cost estimate should reflect this work: compare vendors’ usage-based pricing options side by side, include high and low estimates for the factors most likely to shift costs, and account for data readiness. Incomplete or poorly organized data can reduce the number of tasks AI agents resolve on their own and increase the steps required per outcome. Data quality, therefore, belongs in the cost estimate as well as the technical plan.


The RFP process can support that work. Agencies can ask vendors to show their consumption assumptions, including expected transactions, documents processed, agent runs, peak volumes, and nonproduction use, and to spell out their overage terms. This gives leaders a consistent basis for evaluating proposals.


### Establish contractual and technical guardrails


Contracts should require transparent unit pricing and a clear definition of what each meter measures. Spending thresholds should be tied to obligation ceilings, not just the budget line.


On the technical side, agencies should use native consumption telemetry and alerts where platforms provide them and add external monitoring where they don’t. Some platforms expose detailed usage data but lack configurable alerts or hard spending caps, so governance must also function as an operating process the agency runs. A well-designed alert gives budget owners time to act, for example by flagging that 80% of credits are gone two months into a six-month period.


Guardrails belong in change management, too. Architecture review should require a consumption estimate for every new agent or workflow change before deployment.


### Measure outcomes and optimize continuously


Track cost per mission outcome and report it to CFOs and budget leaders. Show whether AI reduced the cost per successfully resolved case while maintaining service quality, not simply how many credits it consumed.


The same data can drive improvement. Agencies can keep refining models, workflows, data, and routing decisions so that AI consumption becomes a mission investment they can govern and defend.


## Looking ahead


Usage-based pricing is already part of many agencies’ technology portfolios, often alongside the licenses they’ve long managed. The agencies that get the most from AI will treat design choices as cost choices, weighing what can be optimized alongside what’s possible. Leaders can start with one high-value workflow, establish its baseline cost and service quality, test consumption under realistic demand, assign accountability for spending, and scale only when the economics and controls are understood.


By adopting this discipline, leaders can choose the tools and platforms best suited to their missions while keeping costs manageable and operating within federal rules.
